subsubtopic: CALL FOR WITHDRAWAL OF BILL TO ESTABLISH CANAGREX CROWN CORPORATION-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to move a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Bill C-85 will establish a Crown corporation called Canagrex, and the present bill gives this corporation such broad powers that it could, subtly, take over all export business and monopolize same to the detriment of producers and the private sector that is doing a good job and which is capable of expanding to do anything necessary; therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker):
That this House requests the Minister of Agriculture to withdraw the bill or alternatively to delete the clauses proposed in Section 14 and elsewhere in the bill which provide the opportunity for this corporation to become a complete monopoly in the export business.
Canada is a free enterprise country and free enterprise can do the job better than any Crown corporation.

subsubtopic: CALL FOR CERTAIN LIBERAL MEMBERS TO JOIN NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43. Four months ago the first signs of the dissolution of the Liberal Party surfaced when ten Liberal MPs wrote an open letter to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) urging him to adopt new job-creation measures. Then another 15 MPs in a caucus economic development committee sharply criticized the government's economic policy. Now La Presse has revealed that the following Liberals have broken ranks: the hon. members for Sudbury (Mr. Frith), Gloucester (Mr. Breau), Laval (Mr. Roy), Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. McRae), Sherbrooke (Mr. Pelletier), and York South-Weston (Mrs. Appolloni). Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly):
That this House call on the above-named Liberal MPs to stand by their convictions and criticisms by joining the New Democratic Party in terminating the government's budget legislation and thereby terminating the government itself.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to move a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43. It is unjust that freshwater fishermen, who are obliged to pay into the unemployment insurance fund, cannot collect UIC benefits when unemployed. Thousands of freshwater fishermen are not only unable to collect UIC benefits, they are now unable to find work during the off season as a result of the government's total and complete mismanagement of the economy, which is causing severe unemployment across Canada and unbelievable hardship. Unemployment among youth aged 15 years to 24 years, currently running at 16.6 per cent seasonally adjusted, and actually at 18 per cent, is one of the most serious concerns for Canadian society today. speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is to the Solicitor General who, as a lawyer, will know that the purpose of calling character evidence is to lend prestige to the accused through the person or office of the character witness. Will the Solicitor General please confirm that he sent a letter to the lawyer representing Mr. English to be used as character evidence in this particular case, and will he acknowledge the conflict because, as Solicitor General, he and his department are responsible for Mr. English who is now in a penitentiary?

subtopic: CHARACTER REFERENCE GIVEN BY SOLICITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
The hon. member indicated quite clearly in his question that my representation was not made to the judge. I know the individuals concerned and my letter was sent to their lawyer. I told the lawyer that I would be prepared to give evidence on behalf of these people whom I know, and it was on that basis that the letter was put forward. Certainly there was no telephone call, private representation, or off-the-record representation to any court.
The representation was made frankly, on the record, and on behalf of people whom I know.

subtopic: CHARACTER REFERENCE GIVEN BY SOLICITOR GENERAL
speechtext: There is no doubt that it was on the record, and there is no doubt that the judge said it was in poor taste given the Solicitor General occupies the position he does.

speechtext: He is responsible for the parole board, too.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the hon. member is trying to make a clear case of one which is not very clear to me. Surely a minister, like anyone else-
They are not like anyone else.

-should be entitled to give character references on behalf of someone he knows in order to ensure that justice is tempered with mercy. That does not seem beyond the limits of any human being.
Surely it is up to the judge to decide whether he wants to receive such representation or not. Apparently the judge did not. I think this is certainly not the case of a minister trying to influence a judge-
Oh, oh!
-in any way that any citizen is asked to give a character reference.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: He is not any citizen.
He is the Solicitor General.
He is also a human being.
Then he should not be in that cabinet.
If the judge does not want to take into account the testimony of this human being on behalf of one of his fellow Canadians, that is the judge's prerogative.

Madam Speaker, if the Prime Minister does not acknowledge that there is a distinction between a person acting in his own private capacity and when he holds the position of Solicitor General, my question to him is this: since the Solicitor General is responsible for everyone coming into the penitentiary system, and because the

Prime Minister knows that the purpose of good character evidence is meant to minimize sentence, does the Prime Minister not acknowledge that it is inappropriate for a Solicitor General to be giving good character references on behalf of anybody?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext: Madam Speaker, all I can say is that this is not a clearcut case as far as I am concerned. This is not a minister trying to, once again, in an inappropriate way influence a judge. subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR INTRODUCTION OF NEW GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. Since February of this year there have been ten Liberal members from the Montreal area who have indicated that they think that the economic direction of the government is a disaster, 16 Liberal members of the Liberal caucus economic development committee who have expressed a similar concern to that of those ten Liberal members, the Solicitor General who wrote a letter saying that the government's economic policies were a disaster, and we now have the Minister of State for Economic Development reported in today's Le Devoir as indicating that the economic policies being followed by the government are a disaster.
Given that there now appears to be a sense within the Liberal party that what is happening in this country with respect to the economy is heading us in a direction which will cause untold chaos and hardship for tens of thousands of people, can we expect to see a policy put forward by the government before the end of this current session-before the end of June-that will begin to address the problems that confront the one and a quarter million to one and a half million people who are currently unemployed, and the tens of thousands of people who are presently looking to their jobs with considerable trepidation mainly as a result of the government's inability to implement an economic policy which is not a disaster?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR INTRODUCTION OF NEW GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext: Madam Speaker, what surprises me, frankly, is that the opposition seems to be showing great interest in the views of this caucus with regard to the economic situation in Canada.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR INTRODUCTION OF NEW GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext: Everybody is.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR INTRODUCTION OF NEW GOVERNMENT POLICY
speechtext:
Indeed, as the hon. member from the opposition says, everybody is. It would be surprising if members of this caucus, Liberal as they are, were not showing great concern for the rate of unemployment, the high rate of inflation, and for the economic difficulties that the country is going through.
Oral Questions
I appreciate the solicitude shown by opposition members for the views of members of this caucus. I have great interest in those views myself. They are made known to me several times a week, and certainly in caucus every week. Indeed, that is the way this government operates, by soliciting the views of our caucus members and trying to adopt policies which would be beneficial to the country.

REPORTED STATEMENTS MADE BY MINISTER FOR ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, would the Prime Minister care to respond to the statement by the Minister of State for Economic Development, the Senator in the other place? Does he agree with Senator Olson when he says that the major economic thrust of the government was megaprojects, that the high interest rate policy of the government has been the primary factor that undermined the megaprojects, and that there are tens of thousands of jobs which have been lost as a result of the high interest rate policy of the government? If the Prime Minister does agree with him, will he now take steps to bring forward a new policy or, failing that, will he replace the minister?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: REPORTED STATEMENTS MADE BY MINISTER FOR ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I would challenge the hon. member's accuracy when he quotes Senator Olson as talking about high interest rate policies. The Senator knows, as does everyone in the House, that there is no high interest rate policy. There is a high interest rate. That high interest rate is due to the fact that Canada is an open market as far as capital is concerned, and its interest rates cannot be dissociated from the interest rates which prevail on the money markets of the world. That is the reality. It affects Canada, it affects France, it affects Britain, it affects Germany, it affects Italy, it affects Japan-it affects all countries. That does not mean that all of these countries are all seeking to have high interest rate policies; on the contrary, these countries are trying to fight against that high interest rate by having anti-inflation policies.

Is the Prime Minister suggesting that the people of Canada should believe that there is no action which can be taken by the federal government, or by any other government in Canada, to bring down the level of interest rates and thereby safeguard the jobs that they must have in order to provide their livelihood? Is the Prime Minister honestly telling the people of Canada that the policy which has brought about high interest rates and which has destroyed the very opportunities for those people is the only policy the government could follow?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
speechtext: Well, I am not saying that, Madam Speaker. I challenge the hon. member to say whether he was quoting Senator Olson accurately or not.

Yes, I am.

I am.

It was that we lower the value of the dollar, perhaps to 75 cents, perhaps lower-who knows? That might temporarily bring down interest rates. speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: INTERPRETATION OF GUIDELINES GOVERNING MINISTERIAL CONDUCT

Madam Speaker, the hon. member has heard my answer. I did not say "You can influence judges if you do it up front". I said there is a difficult question as to whether a minister can act as a human being or whether he must dissociate himself from that position when he is intervening in a case like the one mentioned by the hon. member. Once again, without refreshing my memory on the guidelines I cannot answer this question with finality. I undertook earlier to look at them. speechtext: That was a low blow.

Mr. Speaker, it is amazing to see how sensitive Liberal members opposite are. They should be sensitive because they bear personal responsibility for the conditions which the young of this country face. This government has mortgaged the future of the young people of this country. What our young people will face in one year, five years or ten years from now is a lifestyle that is substantially diminished because of the personal actions of Liberal backbenchers who are continuing to keep an evil and corrupt cabinet in power. Young Canadians are standing in soup lines today while Liberal backbenchers keep this corrupt and evil government in power. When the government attacks the youth of this nation, it attacks the very future of the nation itself. This Liberal government must be defeated because the future of this nation is at stake.
There is an alternative set of policies which will return Canada to a position of strength and where social justice for all can prevail. 1 will set the scene of Canada's current plight which has been caused by the Liberal government. Other speakers on this side will elaborate on regional problems, on specific industry problems and particularly the problems faced by the youth. We will deal with and we will totally smash the weak and futile arguments which Liberal members put forth. Their pathetic attempts to blame the opposition, to blame the Premiers, to blame the United States and, indeed, to blame Canadians themselves, will be exposed for the hollow and shallow arguments they really are. The fault lies with the Liberal cabinet and Liberal backbenchers. The solution lies in their defeat.
Why is it that today 1.2 million Canadians are unemployed whereas in 1968 only 300,000 people were unemployed? Why is it that youth unemployment today is at 17.5 per cent whereas in 1968 youth unemployment was virtually nil? Why is it that inflation today is at 11.6 per cent whereas in 1968 it was a mere 4 per cent? Why is it that interest rates today are at 15.3 per cent whereas in 1968 they were at 7.5 per cent? Why is it that federal spending is at $74.2 billion whereas in 1968 it was a mere $12 billion? Why is it that the federal deficit is at $50 billion for this year alone-it may be greater-whereas in 1968 it was a mere $500 million? Why is it that the gross national debt is $140 billion whereas it was approximately $30 billion in 1968?
Why is it that we as a nation are paying interest on the national debt of some $16.7 billion this year as compared to
$1.4 billion in 1968? Why is it that the federal government has to advertise to the tune of $250 million to tell people how good the nation is, whereas in 1968 the advertising budget was a mere $29 million? Why were we a strong and vibrant nation in 1968, a nation that had the sense of climbing the mountain and building a future for our young people? When we came out of university at that time why did we have no thoughts of despair and no thoughts of the nation going backwards? We were building a great nation them. That is how it was in 1968.
How did we achieve full employment in 1968? How was it that we had a universal medicare system available to everyone, the poor included? How was it that we had a hospital insurance system that was sound and well funded? How was it that we had a post-secondary education system for our youth who found jobs immediately upon completion of that education? None of us ever thought of unemployment when we came out of university or college in those days. There were five or six jobs for every graduate upon completion of post-secondary education. Even though we had all of these benefits in 1968, we had balanced budgets, we had low taxes and we had true social justice.
The answer to all of my questions is simple. Before 1968 we were not governed by a bunch of socialists. Before 1968 both the Progressive Conservative Party and the Liberal Party believed in individual enterprise rather than state enterprise. We believed in minimal government intervention, government as a regulator rather than as a participant and major player. Wc believed in capital investment by Canadians and by people from other parts of the world. We knew, and we in this party know today, that capital investment means jobs. When there is no capital investment, there are no jobs. Both of the major parties in those days believed that people should be compensated for the risks they take rather than for the position they held, patronage or prior wealth. Only our party believes that today. The situation has changed since 1968. We have a government that has been in power since 1968 and has abandoned individual enterprise for state control and management. The result is exactly the same as in every other country in the world that has tried state centralized control-loss of individual freedoms and loss of choice, which lead to personal despair.
Why is it that Roumania, Poland and the Soviet Union were all massive exporters of food in the early years, but from the time they took to central decision-making and started to get Crown corporations involved they have lost even the capacity to feed their own people? Their people now stand in food lines. That situation is happening here in Canada. We will see more of it. The people who are bearing the brunt of that penalty are the youth of this nation.
Unfortunately, since 1968, and especially now, compensation depends upon prior wealth. You know, Mr. Speaker, the interest to service the national debt is some $16.7 billion. That means people who have wealth in the nation have concentrated into their hands an additional $16.7 billion, which means the rich become incredibly rich. This leads to a class society, which
May 25, 1982

can be seen in other countries that have fabulously rich people and extremely poor people. We know, too, that deficits lead to inflation and with extra money around the value of land goes up. As a result you have a land class and a class without land, the tenants. That is a return to feudalism. What kind of a Parliament and what kind of a government would impose feudalism on the youth of this nation? Our youth will be faced with being tenants and serfs rather than being owners, able to exercise their individual enterprise.
Since 1968 compensation under the Liberal government has depended upon political patronage. One needs only to look at who heads up the Crown corporations, who heads up the advertising and consulting agencies, and who are the heads of boards and commissions. All of these people are paid fabulous salaries and have great indexed pensions. Who are the senior civil servants? All of them have a close tie-in with a small group of men and women who have been running this country since 1968. They are all Liberal party hacks. Most of them were actually turfed out by the electors of the nation. The electors looked at them in their individual constituencies and said that they did not want that man or woman to lead them. They were defeated and then the Liberal government appointed them to very lucrative positions. This is how one gets ahead in 1982 under the Liberal government! It is wrong. It is not what we want for the youth of the nation.
Who suffers under these conditions? Who bears the penalty of inflation or of political appointments? It is ordinary working Canadians-small-business men, farmers, fishermen, senior citizens, and last but not least, it is the future of the country, namely, our youth. We can say goodbye to the just society under the Liberal government.
I will now give some details of the youth situation, which will be followed up by other hon. members on this side. Unemployment in April was some 1,233,000 people, for some 9.6 per cent of the work force. As well there were almost 100,000 men and women who have simply given up. They have just gone home and they are sitting there, awaiting better times, because there is no sense even going out into the market. But more importantly, since August, 1981, over 300,000 jobs which existed then have disappeared at the rate of tens of thousands each week. This will continue for the foreseeable future. Of these 300,000 lost jobs, over 53 per cent were held by young people. Over-all youth unemployment today is 18 per cent.
What is the situation faced by college and university students who need jobs to finance their next year of education? There are simply no jobs available for them. Approximately
190,000	students come out of colleges looking for jobs in the summer and approximately 463,000 out of universities, a total of three-quarters of a million young people looking for jobs to finance their next year of education, so that they are ready, educated and skilled when they complete their education in some two, three or four years. If they cannot find jobs and thus cannot return to school, they sit at home. Their whole attitude toward life is changed or they emigrate to countries where

there are jobs available. This is certainly not in the best interests of Canada.
Beyond the students in universities and colleges, who amount to only 20 per cent of the total youth who start in the school system, 80 per cent of the young people are going out into the work force with grade 12 or less education. What kinds of jobs are available to them? The facts show that the government has reduced research and development so that there are not as many positions available in universities for research or in private corporations because they do not obtain proper tax credits for research and development.
Why are there no jobs for the youth? The answer lies in a long policy-at least since 1968-of state or government intervention in the economy of the nation. I refer to recent policies such as the National Energy Program, which is a nationalization program not a Canadianization one; policies which confiscate wealth from existing corporate enterprises and from individuals who own oil and gas interests; a budget which attacks investors and individual enterprise, whether it is small-business men, farmers, fishermen or individual workers trying to balance their budgets.
The result of these policies within the last few months has been $10 billion of Canadian money flowing out of the country in order for people to purchase shares in companies of other countries. Originally these people may have lived in other lands but they had shares in companies in this country. Approximately $8 billion over and above the $10 billion left this country so that people could purchase shares in United States businesses. They decided that the country was not worth it and that the business climate was wrong. They took their money and purchased shares in United States businesses, in United Kingdom businesses and in businesses around the world. This means that the related jobs are in these various countries rather than here.
Then we can look at the $5 billion to $6 billion each year which leaves the country to buy imported oil. This means that our oil wells in the west, primarily in Saskatchewan and Alberta, are closed in and shut down. Approximately $6 billion flows out of the country to Saudi Arabia, Venezuela, Nigeria and Mexico, which creates jobs in those countries rather than here. We could have $10 billion still working for us here, we could have another $8 billion still working for us here, and we could have $5 billion to $6 billion each year to create jobs for the youth of the nation.
It makes me weep, coming from Alberta, when I return to my riding and observe the oil industry. It once was an industry which created jobs for young people, not for Alberta's youth- there are many jobs still available for them-but for many young men and women from Newfoundland, from the rest of the maritime provinces, from Quebec, Ontario, and in fact from the rest of the country. It was a vibrant industry. Over 700 companies were creating jobs. Well over 90 per cent of the staff of multinational corporations were Canadian men and women, including the upper management of those companies. Indeed, Albertans and other Canadians have gone on to the

The result is that some eight years later they are whipping us in the automobile sales industry. Why not? It goes to show that the government in making its decision did not really understand the ramifications of it and genuinely hurt people. Young people across the nation need to know that they cannot obtain jobs today because of Liberal government decisions of some eight to ten years ago.
How do we create jobs? First, we need a country with resources. Clearly we agree that Canada has plenty in the way of resources. We have oil and gas beyond the wildest dreams of other countries. We have potash, coal, forests, minerals, electricity and a resource we have not even tapped-water. More water flows into the Arctic Ocean than we could use in a million years. It is our ace in the hole.
Second, we need not only a nation with resources, we need people. Canada has the people. We do not have too many people, unlike many other countries with limited resources. For example, Japan, with 122 million people sitting on a rock in the middle of the sea, has some problems. India, with 600 or 700 million people and limited resources, has real problems. In Canada we have 24 million people spread over the assets of an entire half continent. Clearly people are not the problem.

in power. Canadians are greater than the Liberal government that governs them at this moment.
The fifth and prime reason why we are in trouble and have this much unemployment, in spite of our resources and people, is the lack of the business climate which we need. When you examine each individual cabinet minister, you will find that they have no comprehension of business climate, the need for a certain tax structure and for stability in taxation and government policies. The Liberal government has failed miserably. Clearly, the solution is to defeat this government.
The youth of this nation are beginning to discover that this is the remedy. They work hard but 55 per cent of their worth goes into the hands of other people who decide how their money should be spent. They are not happy with this fact and it is a great sign of hope for Canada. The youth of Canada must understand that they need to organize. They will join this party, as they are by the tens of thousands, and we will throw the Liberal backbenchers out riding by riding.
We need a new government which will limit the growth of government and government intervention for reasons other than the ideology that a small group of men and women in Ottawa want to control this nation. It cannot be done. It has never been done in any other country, including those much smaller than Canada.
We need a government which will stress education. When one sees our party's policies, one can see that they are tremendous policies for the development of education. We need to stress research and development and to stress certainty in a solid business climate.
It can be done. A Progressive Conservative government will do it. The youth of Canada are not to be blamed for our problems today, Canadians are not to be blamed and the United States is not to be blamed. It is the Liberal cabinet and individual Liberal Members of Parliament who are responsible for the problems of this nation. Truly, Liberal times are lousy times.

Unfortunately, Mr. Deputy Speaker was engaged in a private conversation with the Clerk of the House at the time and did not hear all the words that were uttered. I advised Mr. May 25, 1982________________COMMONS DEBATES_______________________17737

1 would ask Mr. Deputy Speaker and yourself to undertake to look at the record of the early part of the speech by the hon. member for Lethbridge-Foothills, wherein he stated very clearly that members on this side of the House were voting on legislation and other measures in the House solely to protect their own jobs.
After reviewing the precedents during the last few minutes, this is clearly a breach of privilege of members of the House and it would cast a reflection not only on members on this side but on all members if statements such as that are allowed to continue. I draw your attention to Beauchesne, Citation 316(e) and 316(i). Citation 316(e) states:
Besides the prohibitions contained in SO 35, it has been sanctioned by useage that a member, while speaking, must not-
(e) impute bad motives or motives different from those acknowledged to a
member;
And Citation 316(i) states:
-reflect upon the past acts and proceedings of the House.
If you proceed to Citation 319(3), it states:
In the House of Commons a member will not be permitted by the Speaker to indulge in any reflections on the House itself as a political institution; or to impute to any member or any members unworthy motives for their actions in a particular case; or to use any profane or indecent language; or to question the acknowledged or undoubted powers of the House in a matter of privilege; or to reflect upon, argue against or in any manner call in question the past acts and proceedings of the House, or to speak in abusive and disrespectful terms of an Act of Parliament.
This last point is extremely crucial. It is outlined and documented in Erskine May, 1 believe page 153; there are many cases in British parliamentary history where members may not reflect upon votes which have already taken place in the House of Commons.
Finally, I would draw to your attention page 424 of Erskine May, where it states under the heading "Reflecting upon votes of the House":
The objections to the practice of referring to past debates apply with greater force to reflections upon votes of the House, unless made for the purpose of justifying a motion that the vote be rescinded. Those reflections not only revive discussion upon questions already decided, but are wholly irregular, inasmuch as the member is himself included in, and bound by, a vote agreed to by a majority.
I sincerely feel that this kind of abuse of the rules cannot be allowed to continue if this place is to function in any serious way. We are guilty on all sides of the House of using extreme rhetoric at times to make our case. That is fully acceptable no matter how tiresome it may seem to hon. members and certainly to the public who view us on television each day. However, if this place is to continue to exist and hold the confidence of all Canadians, we must ensure that the rules, procedures and Standing Orders of the House are upheld.
I know the hon. member for Lethbridge-Foothills and I am sure he did not intend to break the rules of the House or reflect

Mr. Speaker, I was a bit unsure whether I would ever get the chance to speak to this motion. With all of the notices of privilege from the other side of the House, I just began to wonder whether or not there was some sort of privilege which would disqualify us from criticizing government policy.
The opposition motion before the House today is a very important one because it is an attempt to focus public attention upon the problem of unemployment among youth across the country. While it is important to discuss unemployment among youth across the country, we cannot, of course, do so in isolation. We must deal with the whole question of unemployment as it affects everyone and which is at such record levels today. When we deal with the question of unemployment among youth, we must deal with the fact that the government of the day is really abdicating its responsibility to manage the economy in a humane and just fashion.
I noted with interest that the first hon. member to speak for the Conservative Party really seemed to indicate that he was in favour of the government continuing to wash its hands of responsibility for economic matters. I guess that is why, when the recent Gallup poll came out asking Canadians whether or not there would be any difference in matters of economic policy if a Conservative government were in office rather than a Liberal government, the majority of Canadians indicated they recognized there would really be no difference. So while it is obviously time to defeat the Liberal government of the day, Canadians will have to look elsewhere for new economic policies and not to the PCs.
The economy today is in one horrific mess. We simply have to remind ourselves of the fact that bankruptcies are at a very high rate. Small businesses are closing daily. Large enterprises are threatened by the present economic recession. Lay-offs continue unabated. These are announced quite regularly and just seem to continue to mount. Mortgages are extremely expensive, so that only a very small percentage of Canadians

can afford to buy a home. Those who presently own homes or who have mortgages are struggling to keep those homes. Many people are having to sell homes for which they have worked and dreamed about for very long periods of time. Government revenues are down because of the present economic recession, and with these revenues down, we begin to get threats to public service salaries. The quality of services which government provides to people is threatened, whether it be in the area of education, health, or in the amount of unemployment insurance available to people. New services are put on hold, whether it be adequate pensions for people or adequate daycare across the country.
The general economic malaise really cuts across all kinds of economic indicators. The one which stands out most, of course, is the fact of unemployment, which is at its highest level since the depression of the 1930s, with over 1.25 million people unemployed today. Things are so bad that even the Liberal caucus seems to begin to recognize the severity of the situation, and not only backbenchers, but also even some cabinet ministers. We recall, for example, the letter from the Quebec MPs who called upon the government to stimulate the economy. I bring to mind the recent document of the Liberal party caucus committee on economic development, which recently became public, pointing out the need for "radically alternative ways of revitalizing the economy and of offsetting the current hard times".
It is in the midst of all this political, social and economic trouble that young people today are graduating from universities, seeking employment and not finding it. Other young people are out of universities for the summer, seeking employment so that they can afford to go back to university in the fall, and are not finding that employment. It is not only those young people who have chosen to go to university who are out of work and who need to work, but, as well, young people who are simply out of work today and who are looking for jobs. We should consider that, of the total number of Canadians unemployed in Canada today, close to half are under 25 years of age. For example, in April's statistics, there were 1,233,000 people unemployed and 508,000, or nearly half of them, were between the ages of 15 and 24. Last month, the seasonally adjusted general rate of unemployment was 9.6 per cent while, on a seasonally adjusted basis, youth unemployment was significantly higher, at 16.6 per cent. If one looks at the unemployment rate among youth on an unadjusted basis, one finds that it was at 18 per cent.
If we take into account the hidden unemployed across this country, those who have simply given up looking for work and who are no longer actively looking for jobs because the jobs are not there, we find that the unemployment rate among young people in this country jumps up to the astronomical figure of 25.1 per cent. We have some 777,000 young people looking for work today. When we add to that the summer students looking for work so they can return to university in the fall as well as the new graduates, the situation is clearly intolerable.

We are threatening the future of this country, making it so difficult for young people today that we are going to rob them of any hope of participating in society in a positive manner. We will rob people of the opportunity to return to university in the fall. Young people are being robbed of the opportunity to contribute to society in a positive way.
Given the severity of the youth unemployment situation, we expected some real innovative and tough action by the government. Instead, we have a government which is clinging to the economic strategy outlined in last November's budget. That budget as an economic instrument is clearly and totally ineffective as we look at the present circumstances, with over a million unemployed as well as the large number of youth who are unemployed.
I wish to review the budget of last November. I think it can be quite fairly described as a tax grab, in the name, ironically, of social justice. It has hurt many ordinary Canadians. It even attempted to tax dental and health plans. The budget had an economic strategy based on energy megaprojects which have now fallen to the ground. They are not going to be the driving force in the economy which the budget anticipated. However, the government has not yet replaced those megaprojects with any other major and important economic stimulus.
The budget of last November cited inflation as the number one problem. Today inflation is continuing to go up and unemployment along with it. In citing inflation as the number one problem, the budget outlined a fiscal and monetary arrangement which would keep interest rates up and ostensibly restrain public expenditures, thereby failing to stimulate the economy. There is no help in the economic policy of the government for the unemployed of this country. There is certainly no real help for those young people who are unemployed.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) made a number of announcements with regard to job measures. I want to highlight one of those announcements. On March 11 this year the minister announced the addition of some $20 million to the summer Canada program, the federal government's student employment program. This was to add
10,000	young people to the employment rolls. It was to bring the total under the federal job employment program this summer up to 53,000 young people.
If we are generous and accept the figures of the government with regard to employment, we should compare that measure with the real need. I wish to refer to a recent article in The Globe and Mail, a well-known, respected and objective journal in this country, dated May 19, 1982. It deals with the question of youth unemployment. The measures of the government pale by comparison with what is needed. I quote from the article:
Employment counsellors and economists cannot remember when the job outlook for students was as dismal as it is this year, and they are predicting that about one-sixth of all students in the labour force this summer will be unable to find work.
One out of every six students will be out of work this summer!

Basically, Mr. Speaker, what the government is doing for student summer employment this summer is just too little. We need further action and we need it now. What the government is doing in regard to unemployment in general is inadequate. With one and a quarter million people unemployed, nearly half of whom are young people, the economic situation is disastrous.
It is time for a new economic strategy. It is time for a new budget. It is time for an adequate program of employment for students. It is time to moderate interest rates. It is time for some economic stimulus so that we can get out of this recession. It is time to stimulate consumer demand which is at an all-time low. It is time, finally, to put in place a long-term industrial strategy that will see Canada processing its natural resources, rather than just selling them off on international markets and leaving Canadians as hewers of wood and drawers of water, and at this time as simply unemployed.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to participate in this debate with respect to youth unemployment. I was particularly impressed by the speech of my colleague, the hon. member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker). He dealt with the government's global economic policies, to which I will refer, but I want to talk also about the government's policies with respect to job training. 1 want to speak about what I consider to be the government's feeble efforts concerning unemployment.
About three or four weeks ago a study was submitted to the government of the province of Ontario and to metropolitan Toronto. This study is entitled "Youth: The Forgotten Generation". The minister and others may be aware of this study. It has to do with skill training and apprenticeship programs in metropolitan Toronto.
It is too early yet for any of the recommendations to be acted upon, but in my opinion this study was important because it clearly identified youth as a group or sector in our society who are suffering far more than we have heretofore understood. We all assumed that certain policies had been carried on by the federal government and by the provincial and municipal governments for a number of years, and we assumed that by and large programs were in place to look after the youth of the country. Therefore, in the natural course of events our youth would be able to enter the labour market and compete well for jobs, not only in this country but throughout the world.
May 25, 1982

This study, and I commend it to the minister, shows that none of that has happened. Despite the minister's huffing and puffing about how well he and his colleagues in cabinet and the federal government do, those things are just not happening.
I will read three paragraphs from this study which show exactly what it means to these people. They are as follows:
To want to work and be unable to find it is painful at any age. but youth unemployment has particular effects, both on the individual and on society. A lengthy period of frustration and enforced idleness when a person first enters the labour force can disable him or her psychologically and in terms of experience for later employment . . . those who encounter serious difficulties in their formative years (from 16 to 24) fail to acquire the experience, training, competence and credentials that would earn them a regular job yielding a reasonable income in their adult years.
In the past society looked to its youth to be the future strength of communities. But even then too many youth were left behind. Now the problem has grown worse. The aged and aging, the training of high-tech workers and other special needs groups gain most of the attention.
Today's youth are being forgotten as we are distracted by continual economic crises and rapidly changing technology. Personal alienation and the risks of social unrest have become substantial and appear to be worsening.
That is a report of four weeks ago. Statistics, particularly as they relate to young people, bear out the grave comments in that report. Youth unemployment rates in this country are double-not just some minor percentage higher-the national average. Unemployment rates are now running close to 18 per cent for people between the ages of 16 and 24.
In 1981, although people between the ages of 16 and 24 made up only 26 per cent of the work force, they accounted for 46 per cent of the unemployed. A total of 238,000 jobs were lost between February, 1981, and March, 1982, and 52 per cent, on 118,000, were jobs held by people between the ages of 18 and 24.
When we talk about youth unemployment, it cannot be dealt with glibly by simply accusing other people of not doing the right thing. Before I outline what I think ought to be done- the minister has heard this before, but despite this he keeps saying that no one puts forward suggestions and continues not to listen-let me say that when we talk about youth unemployment we are not talking about some strange breed of people who do not belong to our society. People between the ages of 16 and 24 do want to work. They want to work for exactly the same reasons that women in our society want to work, for exactly the same reasons that handicapped people in our society want to work and for exactly the same reasons that everyone in our society wants to work.
There are three reasons. They are simple enough that even the minister can understand them. First, people need money to purchase the things they need in order to carry out their responsibilities. Second, people want to make a contribution that is not to be lost. Let me expand on that point. If you find at your very first attempt as a young person entering the work force that no door is open to you-it is not only a question of money because we have social programs which offer some money when people are unemployed-and you find there is no contribution you can make, a scar is formed which lasts a long time. Third, a first job opportunity provides a strong force in the shaping of a human personality.

People want to work, not only for money, not only to make a contribution, but to know who they are. Anyone who raises kids between the ages of 16 and 24-if 1 could call them kids-knows that. Outside of the question of money and contribution, the most important thing they need to know is what kind of people they are. It is probably not appropriate for me to bring in three of the Crombie children who are in that age group. But when young people are looking for employment this summer or looking at what kind of jobs they will get into in their first job in the work force, the single, most important thing they need to know is whether or not they will be able to get a job which will tell them a little bit about who they are. The kind of employment one has determines in large part the kind of person one becomes.
When we talk about youth unemployment, we are not talking about another one of the minister's statistics, nor can the question be dealt with by another one of the minister's announcements. We are dealing here with something very important because we are talking about the first time a person tries to make a connection with the community in terms of contribution, the making of money and the finding out of what kind of a person he or she is.
What is the problem with youth unemployment? It is not complicated. I might say to the minister that there are two elements to it. First, there are not enough jobs. It is that simple, and that is the first reason. There are not enough jobs in this country. The hon. member for Lethbridge-Foothills made it clear that the first thing the minister and the government should understand is that the reason we have youth unemployment is the same reason we have unemployment in every other sector of our society-there are not enough jobs.
People need jobs. That people need jobs is not a complicated theory. The record of the minister's government does not have to be recalled by me. It has been recalled by the hon. member for Lethbridge-Foothills and it will continue to be recalled by every other speaker. It is recalled in the question period daily in this House of Commons and it is mentioned from podiums right across the country. We have a government with an economic record which is the worst we have had in most people's memory, certainly since the depression of the 1930s.
The first problem with youth unemployment is that there are not enough jobs because the government has created an economic climate in which people will not invest. We should not miss the point that people will not invest because they do not trust the goverment to look after their investment. If people do not invest, we will not have jobs. The government's energy policy brought the energy industry to its knees. What it has done in the west it will now do in the east.
The manufacturing sector, which affects employment opportunities in the heartland of the country, in Ontario and Quebec, is also on its knees because of the government's record. I will not go through all the indicators. The minister wishes the boy upon the stairs would go away, but he will not

until the government decides that it is not good enough to put its head in the sand waiting for the Americans to come along with a solution. Also it is not good enough to deny the fact that there is a problem.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Public Works
speechtext: What suggestions do you have?

1 hear a noise over there about suggestions. I have some suggestions. My first suggestion deals with the kinds of jobs which should be related to the educational system. This is a 15-minute debate and 1 only have four minutes remaining, so I will make five suggestions. The first is that the minister ought to consider a change in his understanding of the educational system so that there is a more flexible system of training. Last Friday he brought forward and tabled a training bill. Of course, we will support that bill which deals with training, particularly because the minister and his department have spent so long considering the matter. First there was Bill C-23 and then there was Bill C-67. They are still on the Order Paper, and now we have a new bill. We have not been holding it back; it is the minister. We need to bring back the link between training and work which was lost in the 1960s and 1970s. I might add that it was never brought back together by the federal ministry when it funded all the community colleges in the country. It is time that it was.
Second, we need an apprenticeship program so that there are more in-service rather than pre-service programs. We need to expand, not simply nudge along a little, counselling services in the country. If the minister brings forth anything on counselling he will do good because counselling has failed every neighbourhood, town, village and city in Canada. The link between work and training has been lost as educational systems and schools built up bureaucracies.
Third, there must be co-operation between the federal government and the provinces and municipalities. I should like to refer to an example of what can be done. A certain municipality, a fishing village in Denmark, was faced with a situation where it had some unemployed people. Rather than pay out the amount it would pay for the jobless, it created various jobs. Rather than import the boxes needed to pack fish, it began to hire people between the ages of 18 and 23 to manufacture the boxes. Then they became involved in repairing furniture and toys for schools, particularly for kindergarten classes. They did carpentry work, gardening, recycling projects, painting, and odd jobs; they worked with old people and so on. The point I want to make is that the national government of Denmark did not become involved in the actual operation of the program. It provided some funds which allowed local talent to figure out the best way to do it. This is why time and again we on this
side of the House have insisted it does not matter how much money the minister says he will put into a program, the billions in figures which he uses or how many announcements he makes. He can do it only by co-operation with the provinces and the municipalities. The training bill which he brought forward will only be used in a useful way if the government understands that it cannot be done from Ottawa. The only thing Ottawa can do well is to create an environment within which those who can do the job do it.
Finally, if the government and the minister would announce less, think a little more and try to co-operate a little more, not only would other people trust him but even the minister's department would begin to trust him. Then he would not have to run around trying to figure out where to put ombudsmen to look after their mistakes. We have a situation now where the minister no longer has the support of his own department. He needs to do something soon to re-establish his credibility in the country and certainly in the House. Those of us who represent the rest of the country look forward with anticipation to the debate on the training bill.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the proposals made by the previous speaker, especially concerning in-service or on-the-job training and apprenticeship programs, and I shall be elaborating presently on those very valid proposals which are, in fact, included in the recommendations of the report prepared by the Special Committee on Employment Opportunities for the '80s, under the title "Work for Tomorrow."
First of all, Mr. Speaker, I may point out that it is fairly obvious our present economic situation cannot but have a disastrous effect on youth employment. When the unemployment rate rises among the labour force as a whole, logically, and unfortunately, there is a directly proportional increase in unemployment among young people. In fact, now that the unemployment rate for young people up to the age of 25 revolves around 16.5 per cent, which is twice the national average, it is entirely appropriate that the House should have an opportunity to discuss this extremely important subject.
Not long ago, a Montreal newspaper, following a recommendation by the Quebec Minister of Education that the passing mark in schools be raised from 50 to 60 per cent, reported that young people who were protesting against the minister's recommendation were doing so simply because they had lost confidence in the system and therefore did not see why they should make the required effort at school to obtain a diploma in order to get a job, since they assumed no jobs would be available anyway. I think all this is a reflection of the difficult times we are experiencing today, and that the passing mark debate in Quebec schools-which has a direct connection with today's subject-demonstrates how distressed these young people are about the economic situation and especially about prospects for employment once they finish their schooling. That being said, I believe we must see these things within their

general context. It is true that youth unemployment is excessively high, but perhaps it would also be useful to make a distinction between the percentage due to the economic situation and the percentage due to the very nature of youth unemployment. I may point out that in a study it was shown that between 1976 and 1979, youth unemployment averaged 13.7 per cent, while during the same period, the percentage was 7.2 for adult women and 4.7 for adult men. Furthermore, the turnover rate was 5.9 per cent for young people, but 3 per cent for adult women and 1.8 per cent for adult men. What I am trying to say, Mr. Speaker, is that, although youth unemployment today is twice the rate observed among the labour force in general, this is, in fact, merely a continuation of a trend that was observed earlier and is an indication of the specific labour market adjustment problems found among young people. Not only that, Mr. Speaker, but the same report by the Dodge task force pointed out that 50 per cent of youth unemployment was concentrated among 10 per cent of the youth labour force. In other words, 10 per cent of this population, because of the difficulty they experienced in finding work or adjusting to the labour market environment, represented 50 per cent of the total number of unemployed youth. We have no reason to believe that the situation has changed much today, because the percentages were averaged over five years. And furthermore, when these young people succeeded in finding a job, in 90 per cent of the cases they lost it after a few months. [DOT]
Now, what conclusions should be drawn from these few statistics I have just given you, Mr. Speaker? I can see two. First of all, in today's debate, we must, and 1 have said this before, see these things in their general context, and second, young people are experiencing unemployment and they are being adversely affected by the economic situation, but also by structural problems, namely, the labour market adjustment problems of young people. Consequently, it is imperative that we take this opportunity to find ways of taking corrective action and to seek appropriate solutions to help young people with specific learning problems to enter the labour market. The previous speaker mentioned there were not enough jobs in Canada. That is true but, paradoxically, we have a shortage of skilled manpower, a problem that was already identified in the report by the Special Committee on Employment Opportunities for the '80s. In the House, much has been said, and much more will be said about training, since last Friday the minister tabled Bill C-115, the purpose of which reads as follows, and I quote Section 3:
3. The purpose of this act is to establish a national program to provide occupational training for the labour force and thereby to better meet the need for skills created by a changing economy and to increase the earning and employment potential of individual workers.
I referred just now to the Dodge report, which had ordered a study made in Ontario. It said that out of a sample group of 100 businesses-the study was prepared by the Ontario Ministry of Colleges and Universities-61 per cent of the
Supply
firms had in-house training programs. The firms in question indicated they had no trouble recruiting employees and also that their training programs paid for themselves, because they filled the firm's requirements for skilled manpower. However, of the remaining group of firms included in the study, 84 per cent indicated they had trouble recruiting skilled manpower, 61 per cent indicated they had trouble recruiting employees and finally, they indicated that the only reason why they had no training program was that they did not have the financial resources to do so. In addition, they indicated that they would agree to establish such programs if government assistance were provided. The obvious conclusion is that if the government were to shift the emphasis from its institutional training program, which has been a spending priority to date, to business-as we have started to do, for instance, in the microelectronic sector, and as will probably be done once Bill C-115 has gone through the legislative mill-it would probably be much easier to deal with the labour market entry and adjustment problems experienced by young people who lack the required skills, instead of resorting to direct job-creation programs which are temporary by nature, although certainly useful in the present economic situation, since they provide summer jobs at least for tens of thousands of young people.
In conclusion, we have, on the one hand, a structural breakdown of youth unemployment, and on the other, a functional breakdown of the situation among business firms, namely, the firm that does provide courses or on-the-job training opportunities and the firm that does not. On the one hand, we have a group of young people-the exact present percentage is not available, but according to the study covering the years from 1976 to 1979, this group represents the 10 per cent of unemployed youth which had continuing problems in obtaining employment-which in 1976-79 represented 50 per cent of unemployed youth, and on the other hand, we have businesses that are either reluctant to set up on-the-job training programs or do not have the financial resources but would agree to receiving government financial assistance in setting up such programs. All of this should be seen within the more general perspective that Canada is suffering from a general shortage of manpower for skilled blue-collar-type jobs. To fill these jobs, for many years we have had to import skilled workers such as bricklayers, masons and others from European countries. In fact, if we could manage to train young people for jobs where shortages exist, we would be killing two birds with one stone, namely, filling jobs now available and providing appropriate training for young people who are in desperate straits because they do not have the skills they need to find a job.
Mr. Speaker, I felt these comments were necessary in order to provide a more balanced picture of the unemployment situation, and especially of youth unemployment. To get back to my earlier example which showed young people in Quebec as having lost hope and expressing their bitterness in the

passing mark dispute, 1 want to say that there are jobs for young people who have the required training or who have an opportunity to obtain it. In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I would like to read two relevant recommendations from the report of the Special Committee on Employment Opportunities for the '80s, and herein I support the views of the previous speaker. Recommendation 3 reads as follows:
Governments and the private sector should take steps to correct negative attitudes toward blue-collar trades; to place a high priority on on-the-job training; to provide more instructors (including older workers) for technical training; to make available up-to-date machinery and equipment for training; to reallocate resources to courses offering the greatest employment opportunities; and to establish a continuing education system where an individual can retrain and upgrade throughout a lifetime.
Recommendation 6 reads as follows, and I quote:
Apprenticeship programs should be modernized and expanded to provide for entry at an earlier age, geared to the meeting of standards, not to a time frame open to women and changed to assure completion of course and provide transferable skills.
Mr. Speaker, I support these two recommendations without reservation, and I am convinced that tens of thousands of young people would agree wholeheartedly to take advantage of the opportunities for on-the-job training which could be provided if Bill C-115, tabled in the House by the minister last Friday, is assured a quick passage through this House.
